The '''2022 Kingston upon Thames London Borough Council election''' took place on 5 May 2022 to elect all 48 members of [[Kingston upon Thames London Borough Council]]. The elections took place alongside [[2022 London local elections|local elections in the other London boroughs]] and [[2022 United Kingdom local elections|elections to local authorities across the United Kingdom]].

The [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]] retained overall majority control of the council, the fifth time in the last six elections that the party has won overall control.  

== Background ==
=== History ===
The thirty-two [[London boroughs]] were established in 1965 by the [[London Government Act 1963]]. They are the principal authorities in Greater London and have responsibilities including education, housing, planning, highways, social services, libraries, recreation, waste, environmental health and revenue collection. Some of the powers are shared with the [[Greater London Authority]], which also manages passenger transport, police and fire.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The essential guide to London local government {{!}} London Councils|url=https://www.londoncouncils.gov.uk/who-runs-london/essential-guide-london-local-government|access-date=2021-10-10|website=www.londoncouncils.gov.uk}}</ref>

Since its formation, Kingston upon Thames has been under [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrat]] control, [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] control and [[no overall control]]. The Liberal Democrats have controlled the council since 2002, apart from the period between 2014 and 2018 when the Conservatives had an overall majority. The Liberal Democrats regained control in the [[2018 Kingston upon Thames London Borough Council election|most recent election in 2018]], where they won 39 seats with 51.7% of the vote and the Conservatives won the remaining nine seats with 30.6% of the vote. The [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] lost both seats they were defending and received 11.9% of the vote across the borough.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Holder|first=Josh|title=Local council elections 2018 – results in full|url=http://www.theguardian.com/politics/ng-interactive018/may/04/local-council-election-results-2018-in-full|access-date=2021-10-19|website=the Guardian|language=en}}</ref>

=== Council term ===

A Liberal Democrat councillor, Sharon Falchikov-Sumner, left her party in 2018 after the council voted to close their last residential care home. She joined the [[Green Party of England and Wales|Green Party]] in February 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Rutter|first=Calum|date=2019-02-25|title='We're facing a climate catastrophe' says Kingston councillor|url=https://www.mylondon.news/news/west-london-news/were-facing-climate-catastrophe-says-15885512|access-date=2021-10-19|website=MyLondon|language=en}}</ref> In March 2020, the council leader Liz Green was successfully challenged by Caroline Kerr, a Liberal Democrat councillor who was first elected in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bayley|first=Sian|date=2020-03-24|title=Kingston Council's leader ousted at a key moment in the coronavirus crisis|url=https://www.mylondon.news/news/west-london-news/kingston-councils-leader-been-ousted-17974294|access-date=2021-10-22|website=MyLondon|language=en}}</ref> A Liberal Democrat councillor for Chessington South, Tricia Bamford, resigned in December 2020 due to a change in her family circumstances.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bayley|first=Sian|date=2020-12-01|title=Chessington councillor resigns from Kingston Council|url=https://www.mylondon.news/news/west-london-news/chessington-councillor-resigns-kingston-council-19381531|access-date=2021-10-19|website=MyLondon|language=en}}</ref> A by-election to replace her was not held until 6 May 2021 due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. The by-election, which was contested by thirteen [[Official Monster Raving Loony Party]] candidates, was won by the Liberal Democrat candidate [[Andrew MacKinlay]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Wratten|first=Marcus|date=2021-04-07|title=Chessington South by-election candidates share top priorities in the "forgotten end of the borough"|url=https://kingstoncourier.co.uk/chessington-south-by-election-candidates-share-key-priorities-in-the-forgotten-end-of-the-borough/|access-date=2021-10-19|website=Kingston Courier|language=en-US}}</ref> Mackinlay had previously served as the Labour MP for [[Thurrock (UK Parliament constituency)|Thurrock]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bayley|first=Sian|date=2021-03-03|title=First candidates for Kingston's Chessington South by-election announced|url=https://www.mylondon.news/news/west-london-news/first-candidates-kingstons-chessington-south-19957284|access-date=2021-10-19|website=MyLondon|language=en}}</ref> In September 2021, the Liberal Democrat councillor Jon Tolley left his party due to policy disagreements with the council executive.<ref>{{Cite web|title='We're making a stupid mistake' - Jon Tolley QUITS Kingston Lib Dems|url=https://www.surreycomet.co.uk/news/19564149.jon-tolley-quits-kingston-lib-dems-kingfisher-dispute/|access-date=2021-10-19|website=Surrey Comet|date=7 September 2021 |language=en}}</ref> He announced that he wouldn't contest the next election, saying "I think we were lying to the public" about the demolition of a leisure centre in his ward.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-14 |title=Kingston councillor who quit Lib Dems won't stand in May election |url=https://www.swlondoner.co.uk/news/14032022-kingston-councillor-who-quit-lib-dems-wont-stand-in-may-election |access-date=2022-03-23 |website=South West Londoner |language=en-GB}}</ref> Kerr announced her resignation as council leader in October 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kingston Council leader Caroline Kerr resigns|url=https://www.surreycomet.co.uk/news/19657901.kingston-council-leader-resigns/|access-date=2021-10-22|website=Surrey Comet|date=19 October 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

As with most London boroughs, Kingston upon Thames was electing its councillors under new boundaries decided by the [[Local Government Boundary Commission for England]], which it produced after a period of consultation. The number of councillors remained at 48, but the commission produced new boundaries following a period of consultation, with ten three-member wards and nine two-member wards.<ref>{{Cite web|title=LGBCE {{!}} New political map for Kingston upon Thames Council {{!}} LGBCE Site|url=http://www.lgbce.org.uk/media/new-political-map-for-kingston-upon-thames-council|access-date=2021-10-19|website=www.lgbce.org.uk|language=en}}</ref>

== Electoral process ==
Kingston upon Thames, like other London borough councils, elects all of its councillors at once every four years. The previous election took place in 2018. The election took place by multi-member [[first-past-the-post voting]], with each ward being represented by two or three councillors. Electors had as many votes as there are councillors to be elected in their ward, with the top two or three being elected.

All [[Elections in the United Kingdom#Registration procedure|registered electors]] ([[British citizen|British]], [[Irish citizen|Irish]], [[Commonwealth citizen|Commonwealth]] and [[European Union]] citizens) living in London aged 18 or over were entitled to vote in the election. People who lived at two addresses in different councils, such as university students with different term-time and holiday addresses, were entitled to be registered for and vote in elections in both local authorities.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=How the elections work {{!}} London Councils|url=https://www.londoncouncils.gov.uk/who-runs-london/london-elections/how-elections-work|access-date=2021-09-14|website=www.londoncouncils.gov.uk}}</ref> Voting in-person at polling stations took place from 7:00 to 22:00 on election day, and voters were able to apply for postal votes or proxy votes in advance of the election.<ref name=":1" />
